extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy (readers of treatises on syllogism and inference)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and construct categorical syllogisms and related forms of ratiocination: assess premises (definition vs fact), term-usage, conversion/obversion rules, singular vs universal propositions, and alternative formalizations (numerically definite propositions, quantification of predicate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definition from factual assertion in premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The major premise (definition) must be distinguished from a statement of fact; a definition can be true while a factual minor premise is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example with dragons: if 'A dragon is a thing which breathes flame' is understood as a definition it differs from asserting as fact that 'a dragon breathes flame.' Predicating a real property of an imaginary creature implicitly asserts its reality; to avoid this change the predicate to something like 'imagined as breathing flame.' The conclusion must be formed with predicates that preserve whether the subject is real or imagined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocation — check multiple senses of key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that seem to turn wholly on words often depend on varied 'shades of meaning' of leading terms; a critic lacking knowledge of the relevant Things may mistake a valid inference for a fallacy of equivocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'sagacious and penetrating mind' can find unobvious links between different senses and validly infer across them; beware of the anti-pattern of dismissing an argument as merely verbal when it rests on subtle substantive connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust predicates when subject may be imaginary
rubrics_metrics.description: When a subject can be real or imaginary, predicates asserting actual properties should be rephrased so as not to assert reality (e.g., 'imagined to breathe flame').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to alter predicates leads to hidden assertion of existence. Use modifications that explicitly mark imagined/non-real status when premises concern imagined entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obversion and equivalent propositional forms
rubrics_metrics.description: One common change of expression is from affirming a proposition to denying its negative (obversion); equivalent propositional forms (equipollency) can be used for immediate inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: Professor Bain's treatment of 'Equivalent Propositional Forms' and the use of obversion as a standard transformation for converting propositions while preserving logical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion forms and cautious rephrasing (Hamilton's example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions admit conversion into non‑standard forms (e.g., 'Some A is not B' -> 'No B is some A'), but such forms may require care in interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: 'Some men are not negroes; therefore, No negroes are some men (e.g., Europeans).' These rephrasings can be formally correct yet misleading if one does not attend to the intended scope and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize oppositional relations among propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify categorical relations correctly: Contraries (All A is B / No A is B), Subtraries (Some A is B / Some A is not B), Contradictories (All A is B / Some A is not B; No A is B / Some A is B), and subaltern relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classifications to determine valid immediate inferences and the mutual entailments or incompatibilities among categorical statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat singular propositions carefully vs universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions (e.g., 'Socrates is wise') have a contested status: if the predicates are part of the meaning of the proper name, no real inference occurs; if the premises are real and independent, a syllogistic conclusion may be genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two illustrated cases: (1) If attributes are connoted by the name, listing them is mere repetition (no inference). (2) If premises are independent facts ('Socrates was the master of Plato' and 'Socrates fought at Delium'), forming 'The master of Plato fought at Delium' can be seen as an equivalent form or an inference that omits part of the original conjunctive information. Beware the anti-pattern of treating all singular-premise syllogisms as non-inferential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for partial coincidence when transferring attributes (Bain's objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiom that 'an attribute A coincides with attribute B' must allow for the fact that terms may be co-extensive only in part; logic must provide for limitation when transferring A to C through an intermediary B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A carries B and B carries C, but other things also carry B; one must perform a process of limitation rather than assume co-extensiveness and conclude A and C are co-extensive. The Conversion rules and ordinary knowledge of language normally prevent misreading, but formal treatments must make limitation explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major and minor premises are practical safeguards, not necessary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllogistic major and minor are conveniences for expressing the reasoning, not strict conditions required for the inference itself; reasoning can proceed without them, but they prevent error by specifying the kind of likeness required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true minor needed for inference is that 'Socrates is like A, B, C' (i.e., like observed cases). The major specifies what kind of likeness is sufficient to apply the predicate. Use majors/minors as explicit checks that the particular case meets the type of resemblance relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerically definite propositions (De Morgan) are formally valid but often impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences from premises like 'most Bs are Cs' can be made precise by specifying numerical proportions (e.g., 60% and 70% entail at least 30% overlap), allowing rigorous formulæ for many particular forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such 'numerically definite syllogisms' are legitimate and interesting, they are rarely useful in ordinary reasoning because the empirical premises typically lack numerical precision. They are valuable pedagogically but limited for practical argument testing outside probabilistically precise contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of the predicate (Hamilton) changes propositional content
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifying the predicate (e.g., 'All A is all B' or 'Some A is some B') produces new formal forms and yields different syllogistic rules, but may not reflect the speaker's actual thought or the ordinary meaning of propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton's system yields a unified canon and expanded set of legitimate moods, and can serve as a correctness test since ordinary propositions can be translated into predicate-quantified forms. However, the quantification often 'leads the mind out of the proposition' into a different order of ideas and may be 'superfluous or erroneous' for analyzing mental processes of reasoning. Use with caution when modeling actual thought processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express general propositions as 'any' to reflect inductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: To better represent induction as inference from particulars to particulars, general propositions used in reasoning might be phrased 'Any man is mortal' rather than 'All men are mortal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing highlights that general propositions function to vouch for the legitimacy of particular-to-particular inferences, making explicit that reasoning from experience is grounded in observed particulars rather than a prior universal that 'proves' an individual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the verbal paradox of a general premise proving its components
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an abuse of language to claim that the proof that Socrates is mortal is 'All men are mortal' taken alone; both the general and particular assertions are supported by the same grounds of experience rather than one proving the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine arguments that treat the major premise as an independent proof of the minor; instead, view both as interpretations of the same experiential evidence. The minor serves to show that the particular meets the resemblance specified by the major.
